html:
The Treaty of El Pardo of 1778 was signed by Spain and Portugal; Portugal handed Spain the islands of Fernando Po and Annobón and trading rights on the nearby mainland coast.

It was part of a settlement of their quarrels over land in South America. Spain wanted a source of enslaved workers of its own, but its first expedition to Fernando Po was wrecked by fever and revolt, and it did little there for decades.

The treaty is still the root of the country's shape: an island capital, a small mainland territory, and the Spanish language. It made Spanish Guinea the only Spanish colony south of the Sahara, and Equatorial Guinea the only Spanish-speaking state in Africa. Portugal kept nearby São Tomé.
